title: Why 'Hot Hands' in Basketball Were Actually Real & Why Casino Gamblers Fall for the Opposite Illusion — Gilovich (1985) vs. Miller & Sanjurjo's (2018) Econometrica Bias Theorem, 1913 Monte Carlo's 26 Blacks & Human Dopamine D2R/D3R (PDB 8TZQ, 6CM4, 7CMU)

teenKit.tldr: Textbooks claimed the basketball "hot hand" was a myth for 33 years, but a 2018 mathematical correction proved real streaks actually exist. Meanwhile, our brains stubbornly fall for the exact opposite illusion—the Gambler's Fallacy—when facing random chance.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our dopamine receptors and brains misread streaks explains why human intuition constantly struggles against math, whether you're sinking hoops or avoiding a roulette wheel.
keyTakeaways: For 33 years, a famous 1985 study convinced scientists that basketball hot streaks were an optical illusion caused by human pattern-seeking.
A 2018 math correction published in Econometrica proved that looking at streaks through small sample sizes actually hid the real hot hand (+8 to +13 percentage points boost).
Human brains are wired by dopamine receptors (D2R/D3R) to crave patterns, which drives both the euphoria of sports momentum and the financial trap of the Gambler's Fallacy.

vocab.meaning: The mistaken belief that a streak of success means future success is guaranteed, or conversely, the 33-year scientific consensus that denied real sports momentum.
The false gut feeling that if a coin lands on heads five times in a row, tails is somehow "due" to happen next.
A mathematical trap where looking at short bursts of random events accidentally erases the actual trends hiding inside them.
Microscopic protein locks on your brain cells that process reward, motivation, and the thrill of chasing a win.

quiz.question: What did Joshua B. Miller and Adam Sanjurjo discover in their 2018 Econometrica paper?
options: Basketball players actually shoot worse when they are tired.
The original 1985 study missed a math bias, and hot streaks in basketball are mathematically real.
Roulette wheels in Monte Carlo can be rigged by tracking the ball's speed.
Dopamine receptors completely shut down after three consecutive successes.
quiz.explanation: Their finite-sample selection-bias theorem proved that the 1985 study's math accidentally hid real shooting streaks.

quiz.question: What is the Gambler's Fallacy?
options: Believing that past random events alter the probability of future independent random events.
Assuming that a hot player will never miss a single shot.
The medical condition caused by taking too many Parkinson's disease medications.
A structural defect in 1-Angström protein crystals.
quiz.explanation: The Gambler's Fallacy tricks your brain into thinking a coin or roulette wheel is "due" to change after a streak, ignoring that odds reset every single time.

quiz.question: Why does the podcast connect basketball stats to Swedish Parkinson's disease registries and dopamine receptors?
options: To show that professional basketball players have higher rates of neurological disorders.
To prove that cold weather changes how basketballs bounce on a court.
To link the brain's physical reward chemistry and dopamine pathways to how humans process risk, streaks, and addiction.
To demonstrate that computers can predict free throws better than humans.
quiz.explanation: The episode bridges high-level math with microscopic brain chemistry to show how our neural hardware drives our obsession with streaks and chance.
